title: DLMF 25.10 Zeros: The product representation ( 25.2.11 ) implies \zeta\left(s\right)\neq 0 for \Re s>1 .
summary: DLMF 25.10 Zeros: The product representation ( 25.2.11 ) implies \zeta\left(s\right)\neq 0 for \Re s>1 .
body:
NIST DLMF section 25.10 (Zeros) says: "The product representation ( 25.2.11 ) implies \zeta\left(sight)
eq 0 for \Re s>1 . Also, \zeta\left(sight)
eq 0 for \Re s=1 , a property first established in Hadamard ( 1896 ) and de la Vallée Poussin ( 1896a , b ) in the proof of the prime number theorem ( 25.16.3 ). The functional equation ( 25.4.1 ) implies \zeta\left(-2night)=0 for n=1,2,3,\dots . These are called the trivial zeros . Except for the trivial zeros, \zeta\left(sight)
eq 0 for \Re s\leq 0 . In the region 0<\Re s<1 , called the critical strip , \zeta\left(sight) has infinitely many zeros, distributed symmetrically about the real axis and about the critical line \Re s= rac{1}{2} . The Riemann hypothesis states that all nontrivial zeros lie on this line. Calculations relating to the zeros on the critical line make use of the real-valued function is chosen to make Z(t) real, and \operatorname{ph}\Gamma\left( rac{1}{4}+ rac{1}{2}itight) assumes its principal value. Because |Z(t)|=|\zeta\left( rac{1}{2}+itight)| , Z(t) vanishes at the zeros of \zeta\left( rac{1}{2}+itight) , which can be separated…" Equation 25.10.1 on the page has alt text "Z(t)\equiv\exp\left(i\vartheta(t)ight)\zeta\left(	frac{1}{2}+itight),". Equation 25.10.2 on the page has alt text "\vartheta(t)\equiv\operatorname{ph}\Gamma\left(	frac{1}{4}+	frac{1}{2}it% ight)-	frac{1}{2}t\ln\pi".
